unit.title: Cut fit and install trunking system

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. You may use a calculator. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: When planning a trunking route through an existing office, what should be found out first?
options: The cheapest colour of trunking in the catalogue
Where each member of staff likes to sit
Obstacles, other services and fire walls
The time of the office's next staff meeting

questions.stem: A 75 mm × 38 mm trunking may be filled to 45% of its inside area. What is the most cable area it may hold?

3375 mm²

questions.stem: A trunking with an inside area of 2500 mm² holds cables with a total area of 900 mm². What percentage of it is filled?

questions.stem: A length of trunking costs J$2 800, and a job needs 12 lengths. What is the cost of the trunking before GCT?

options: Burning PVC gives off toxic fumes

options: Before painting, so the paint covers it too

questions.stem: A trunking lid keeps springing off a run fixed to an uneven block wall. What is the best fix?
options: Wrap tape around the lid and base

options: Nothing, as trunking keeps cables cool

questions.stem: A PVC trunking run in a hotel lobby needs ten 90° flat bends. Which is best?
options: Make each one by cutting with a knife
Leave neat gaps at every corner

options: On a scrap of paper kept in the van

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show any working. You may use a calculator. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the trunking fitted along a wall at desk height, often with separate compartments for power and data outlets?
A trunking measures 75 mm × 50 mm inside. What is its inside area, in mm²?
What term is used for the number, from a maker's table, given to each cable and each trunking size so you can work out how many cables fit?
What is the name of the fitting used where a trunking run turns into the inside corner between two walls?
Steel trunking for damp places is often given a zinc coating to stop rust. What is this coating process called?
Which instrument is used to check the earth continuity of a steel trunking run?
What is the name of the threaded steel bar used to hang trunking from a ceiling?
What word describes PVC that has become hard and cracks easily after years in strong sunlight?
Trunking comes in 3 m lengths. How many lengths are needed for a straight 25.5 m run, with no allowance for waste?
What do the letters UV stand for, the part of sunlight that damages plastics?
What is the name of the trunking laid in or under a floor, with outlet boxes at set points?
What is the name of the part inside multi-compartment trunking that keeps the compartments apart?
The cables in a run have a total cable factor of 420, and the trunking factor is 700. What percentage of the trunking's capacity is used?
What do we call the list of all the materials needed for a job, with quantities, prepared from the drawings before ordering?
Name a hand tool used to remove the sharp burr from the cut edges of steel trunking.

essays.stem: Your team will install trunking for power and data in a new 30-seat computer lab at a school in Mandeville. Explain how you would plan the installation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would study the drawings and specification, then survey the room: wall materials, the positions of desks, windows, doors, the board and any fire walls or other services in the way. I would choose the type of trunking, such as two-compartment dado trunking, so power and data are segregated. I would list every cable that will go in each section, work out the space needed using the maker's cable factors or the fill limit in the specification, and choose a size with room for future cables. I would plan the route, the height from the finished floor, the fittings (angles, tees, outlet boxes with dividers, end caps) and how it enters the board, and check the support spacing from the maker's data. Then I prepare a take-off with quantities and a waste allowance and order early. I plan safe isolation of any existing circuits, the access equipment, the order of work with other trades, the inspection and tests, and how the work is shared in the team.
markingPoints: Studies drawings and surveys the room, services and fire walls
Chooses a suitable segregated trunking type
Works out capacity from cable factors or fill limit, with spare room
Plans route, height, fittings, board entry and supports; prepares a take-off
Plans isolation, access, sequencing, inspection, tests and team roles

essays.stem: A run must hold 30 cables of 2.5 mm² (cable factor 12 each) and 12 cables of 4 mm² (cable factor 16 each). A maker's table gives these trunking factors (example figures): 50 × 38 mm = 738; 50 × 50 mm = 1037; 75 × 50 mm = 1555. Work out which size to use, and explain your choice.
essays.modelAnswer: First I add up the cable factors. For the 2.5 mm² cables: 30 × 12 = 360. For the 4 mm² cables: 12 × 16 = 192. The total is 360 + 192 = 552. Next I compare this with the trunking factors. The trunking factor must be equal to or greater than the total cable factor. The 50 × 38 mm trunking has a factor of 738, which is greater than 552, so it would just hold the cables. However, it would be about 75% of its capacity, leaving little room for future cables and making it hard to lay cables in neatly. The 50 × 50 mm trunking, with a factor of 1037, would be about half full, leaving room for extra circuits later. So I would choose 50 × 50 mm, unless the specification asks for more spare space. I would also remind the designer that many cables grouped together need their current ratings reduced, which may change the cable sizes.
markingPoints: Correct factor for 2.5 mm² cables: 360
Correct factor for 4 mm² cables: 192, total 552
Compares with the trunking factors correctly (trunking factor at least the cable total)
Chooses 50 × 50 mm with a reason (spare capacity)
Mentions grouping and derating of cables

essays.stem: Describe how to install a steel trunking system with a site-made bend, a tee and an entry into a distribution board, including how earth continuity is kept and checked.
essays.modelAnswer: With the board isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead, I mark the route level or plumb and fix the supports at the maker's spacing. I measure and mark each length from the plan, cut square with a fine-tooth hacksaw, and file off every burr. For a site-made 90° bend, I mark and cut a V out of the sides, bend the base, fit a backing plate and rivet or bolt it, and file the edges smooth. The tee is a factory fitting fixed with couplers. Lengths are joined with couplers, and a copper earth link is fitted across every joint unless the maker states the coupler itself gives continuity. At the board, a flanged adaptor is used so the edges are covered and the trunking is bonded to the board. Holes for conduit or cable exits get grommets or bushes. After installation, and before cables go in, I test the earth continuity from the board's earth bar to the far end and across each joint with a low-resistance ohmmeter, and record the readings.
markingPoints: Safe isolation of the board before working at it
Supports at maker's spacing; accurate marking, square cuts, deburring
Correct site-made bend method
Couplers with earth links; flanged board entry; grommets at holes
Earth continuity tested end to end and across joints, and recorded

essays.stem: Explain how segregation and fire safety are achieved in a trunking system that carries power, data, fire alarm and emergency lighting cables through several rooms.
essays.modelAnswer: Segregation means keeping different systems apart. Multi-compartment trunking is used, with dividers that continue through every bend, tee and outlet box, so power cables cannot touch data cables or the fire alarm and emergency lighting cables. Fire alarm and emergency lighting circuits are often kept in their own compartment or system, so a fault or fire in the power cables does not damage them, and they use fire-resistant cable as the design says. Where cables of different voltages share a compartment, all must be insulated for the highest voltage present. Compartments are labelled at access points. For fire safety, where the trunking passes through a fire-rated wall or floor, a fire barrier is fitted inside the trunking and the gap around it is sealed with fire-stopping, so fire and smoke cannot pass. After extra cables are added, the fire stopping is made good. PVC trunking is not used where it could add to a fire or give off smoke in escape routes if the specification forbids it.
markingPoints: Multi-compartment trunking with continuous dividers
Fire alarm and emergency lighting kept separate and in fire-resistant cable
Insulation for the highest voltage when circuits share; compartments labelled
Fire barriers and fire-stopping at fire walls and floors
Fire stopping made good after changes; material choice in escape routes

essays.stem: Choose the most suitable trunking system for each of these places, and explain your choices: a hotel kitchen, a beach-front bar in Negril, and an air-conditioned office.
essays.modelAnswer: In the hotel kitchen, heat, steam, grease and cleaning are the main problems. I would choose steel trunking with a suitable coating, or stainless steel, kept away from the hottest spots over the cooking range, because PVC could soften near the heat. Lids must fit well to keep grease out, and the system must be earthed. At the beach-front bar, salt air and strong sun are the problems. Ordinary steel would rust quickly and indoor PVC could go brittle in the sun. I would choose a UV-resistant PVC system made for outdoor use, or stainless steel, with stainless fixings, and keep it under the roof where possible. In the air-conditioned office, the conditions are mild and appearance and flexibility matter. I would choose PVC dado trunking with separate compartments for power and data, which looks neat, is easy to add outlets to, and does not need earthing. In each case I would follow the specification and the maker's data.
markingPoints: Kitchen: heat, steam and grease named; steel or stainless chosen, away from heat
Bar: salt air and UV named
Bar: UV-resistant outdoor PVC or stainless with suitable fixings
Office: PVC dado trunking with segregated compartments, with reasons
Refers to specification and maker's data

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect and test a finished trunking installation before handover, and what you would do about defects.
essays.modelAnswer: I inspect the whole run against the drawing and specification. I check it is on the right route, level or plumb, and at the right height; that all fixings are secure at the right spacing; that cut edges are smooth with no burrs; that joints, bends and tees are neat with no gaps; and that lids fit along the whole length. Inside, I check the cables are not over-filled, pinched or damaged, are held by retainers on vertical and ceiling runs, and that segregation dividers are continuous and compartments labelled. I check grommets at every exit, the board entry, and fire barriers and fire stopping at fire walls. For steel trunking, I check earth links are fitted and, with a low-resistance ohmmeter, test the earth continuity end to end and across joints, and record the readings. Every defect is listed with its location, put right by the team, then rechecked. The inspection checklist and test results are signed and handed over with the as-built drawing.
markingPoints: Checks route, level, height and fixings against drawings
Checks cut edges, joints, fittings and lids
Checks cables, fill, retainers, segregation and labels
Checks grommets, board entry and fire stopping; tests earth continuity
Lists defects, has them fixed and rechecked, and records and hands over results

essays.stem: Explain how heat, sunlight and salt air can affect a trunking system in Jamaica, and how a good installation allows for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat makes PVC trunking expand: a long run in a hot roof space or in sun can grow by several millimetres, and if it cannot move it bows or pulls out its fixings. To allow for this, expansion couplers or small gaps at joints are used on long runs, as the maker advises, and fixings let the trunking slide. Heat also reduces how much current the cables inside can carry, so the designer applies rating factors. Strong sunlight contains ultraviolet light, which makes ordinary PVC brittle over time, so it cracks. Outdoor runs should use UV-resistant material made for outdoor use, or be placed in shade. Salt air near the coast makes ordinary steel rust quickly, and rusted joints can lose their earth continuity. Near the sea, galvanised, coated or stainless steel trunking with matching fixings is used, cut edges are treated, and earth continuity is checked during maintenance. Choosing the right material for each place makes the system last.
markingPoints: Heat causes PVC expansion; allowed for with expansion couplers or gaps
Heat reduces cable current rating; rating factors applied
UV makes PVC brittle; UV-resistant material or shade used
Salt air rusts steel and can break earth continuity
Galvanised, coated or stainless steel with treated edges and checks

essays.stem: As the Level 3 member, you lead three trainees installing PVC and steel trunking in a training block. Explain how you would brief, supervise and check their work.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work, I brief the trainees on the drawing, the route and heights, the fittings to use, and the quality I expect, and I show them a good example of a mitred joint and a steel joint with an earth link. I give a safety briefing: safe isolation of any circuits nearby, using a cable detector before drilling, safe use of ladders or the tower, eye and dust protection, and gloves for steel edges. I share out the work so each trainee has a section and can learn, and pair the least experienced with me at first. I check the first length each trainee fixes for level, fixings and edges before they continue, then spot-check as they go. I set hold points: before cables go in, I check deburring, joints, earth links and retainers; before lids go on, I check the cables are not pinched and segregation is kept. I give clear, positive feedback, have any defects corrected, and record the inspection and tests.
markingPoints: Briefs on drawing, standard and fittings with a demonstration
Gives a safety briefing (isolation, detector, access, PPE)
Shares work for learning and pairs where needed
Checks first work, spot-checks and uses hold points before cables and lids
Gives feedback, has defects corrected and records inspection and tests

essays.stem: Your team must extend an existing trunking system in an occupied office and add new circuits into it. Some of the trunking already carries working circuits. Explain how you would plan and carry out the work safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first find out from the drawings and by checking on site which circuits run in the trunking and which boards feed them. I agree with the client a time when those circuits can be switched off, because I will not open trunking or work among cables that are live. At that time, each circuit is switched off, locked off and tagged, with each worker's own lock, and proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Computers and other equipment on those circuits are shut down properly first. The work area is coned off and staff are kept away from ladders and tools. We fix the new trunking, join it to the old run with proper fittings and earth links if it is steel, and lay in the new cables without damaging the old ones, keeping segregation. Any fire stopping we disturb is made good. The new circuits are tested, the old ones checked, locks removed, and the client is told when power is back. The drawings are updated.
markingPoints: Identifies the circuits in the trunking and their boards
Agrees a shut-down time; never works among live cables
Isolates, locks, tags and proves dead with a checked tester; equipment shut down first
Protects office staff; joins and earths correctly; keeps segregation and fire stopping
Tests, restores supply safely, informs the client and updates drawings

essays.stem: Explain how you would work out the materials and their cost for a trunking job from a drawing, using this example: 26 m of 50 × 50 mm trunking in 3 m lengths at J$2 800 each, plus 4 internal angles at J$650, 2 tees at J$900 and 2 end caps at J$250.
essays.modelAnswer: I measure every run on the drawing using its scale, and check the measurements on site if I can. Then I count every fitting: angles, tees, end caps, couplers and outlet boxes. For the trunking, I add about 10% for waste: 26 × 1.1 = 28.6 m. Divided by 3 m lengths, this is 9.53, so I order 10 lengths. 10 × J$2 800 = J$28 000. The fittings are: 4 angles × J$650 = J$2 600; 2 tees × J$900 = J$1 800; 2 end caps × J$250 = J$500. That makes J$4 900 for fittings. The total for these materials is J$28 000 + J$4 900 = J$32 900. I would then add the fixings, couplers, earth links and any other items, the firm's mark-up as its policy says, and GCT at the current rate on the total before tax. I set the take-off out as a table and check it with a quick estimate, so another person can check it.
markingPoints: Measures runs from the scaled drawing and counts every fitting
Adds a waste allowance and rounds up to 10 lengths
Trunking cost J$28 000 and fittings J$4 900 worked out correctly
Total J$32 900, then adds other items, mark-up and GCT at the current rate
Sets out as a table and checks it

practical1.title: Plan and install a two-compartment PVC dado trunking system with segregated power and data outlets
practical1.brief: As a group, plan and install a two-compartment PVC dado trunking system along two walls of a training bay, with one internal angle, one external angle, a tee to a short vertical drop, two outlet boxes with dividers and end caps, from the drawing given by the assessor. First, prepare a take-off list with a waste allowance, and a capacity check for the cables the drawing lists (using the maker's cable factors or the fill limit given), and mark out the route at the drawing height with a level and chalk line. Use a cable detector before drilling. Share the work so every member measures, cuts and fixes at least one length or fitting, while another member checks it. Lay in the power and data cables in their own compartments, with the divider continuous through every fitting, and label the compartments. A member who did not install a section inspects it against the checklist before the lids go on. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Two-compartment PVC dado trunking with lids, internal and external angles, a tee, end caps and two outlet boxes with dividers
Short lengths of power cable and data cable for laying in
Fine-tooth hacksaw, mitre box, file, tape measure, try square, spirit level and chalk line
Cable detector, hammer drill, masonry bits, wall plugs and round-head screws with washers (or the bay's fixing board)
Cable factor table or fill limit, take-off sheet and inspection checklist from the assessor
Safety glasses, dust masks and ear protection
photos: The take-off list and capacity check
The route marked out level at the drawing height
The cable detector in use before drilling
The internal and external angles and the tee fitted, close up
Power and data cables in separate compartments, with the divider continuous through a fitting
The finished run with lids on and compartments labelled
checklist: Took part in the take-off and capacity check, with correct working
Measured, marked and cut their length or fitting square and accurately
Fixed the base level and secure at the spacing given
Made neat joints and fitted fittings with no gaps or sharp edges
Kept power and data segregated, with the divider continuous
Inspected another member's section and recorded the result
Used the cable detector and PPE, and left the area clean with off-cuts sorted
safety: Use a cable detector before drilling, and do not drill near marked services
Wear safety glasses and a dust mask when cutting and drilling, and ear protection with the hammer drill
Use stepladders as the Centre's rules say, with a second person footing them
No circuit is connected in this task; cables are laid in dead

practical2.title: Install a steel trunking system with a site-made bend, a vertical riser and a board entry, and test its earth continuity
practical2.brief: As a group, install a galvanised steel trunking system on the training wall from the drawing given by the assessor: a horizontal run with one site-made 90° flat bend, a factory tee, a vertical riser with cable retainers, and a flanged entry into an unpowered training distribution board. Before work at the board, it is isolated, every member fits their own lock and tag, and it is proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Plan first: mark the route, set the support spacing from the maker's data, and write a short method for the site-made bend. Share the work so every member does at least one task (marking and cutting, the site-made bend, fixing supports, fitting couplers and earth links, fitting the riser retainers, the board entry) while another member checks it. File every cut edge and fit grommets at any exit hole. Then test earth continuity with a low-resistance ohmmeter from the board's earth bar to the far end and across each joint, record the readings, and mark the as-built route on the drawing. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Galvanised steel trunking and lids, a tee, couplers, end caps, copper earth links and a flanged board adaptor
